Discuss the equity issues that effect our educational system. Elaborate in your own words.
Views
   ● Inequities have badly affected our education system and not only in Pakistan but many
       other countries are facing this problem. Along with with human development, the number
       of Inequities is increasing on a daily basis as mentioned below;
   1. Poverty: Our biggest problem is poverty. This is affecting the education system badly.
       Even after 75 years of independence, we haven't been able to overcome poverty. But
       poverty can be eradicated through education.
   2. Silent emission: Here we have an equity issue is silent exclusion. If you never come to
       school you are excluded and drop out.
   3. Income: is becoming very problematic for a common man nowadays. We have more
       problems than resources which are increasing day by day.
   4. Gender: is also an equity issue in education system. That's why Girls enrollment ratio is
       very less than boys
   ● There are many more issues here but I move towards the end of my topic.
   ● Finally, I would like to say that we have to ensure the availability of basic and necessary
       resources for the betterment of a child's future. Moreover, for the improvement of the
       education system, new syllabus, modern teachers training, best educational activities,
       clean environment of educational institutions, provision of health facilities, free quality
       education, uniform and possible scholarships should be ensured. By which our society
       will grow.

Lesson 1. Introduction to Contemporary Trends and Issues and National and International
                                     Conventions on Education

Topic 1: Education in twenty first Century

In the title of the course there are three (3) key terms.

    1. Contemporary
    2. Trends
    3. Issues

These three terms can be explained like as under.

    1. Contemporary

   Contemporary means related to the present time or starting as of today. What we experience in
education today.

    2. Trends

   Are positive kinds of things that are happening in other words the patterns that we like to see and
continue.

    3. Issues

    Issues deal with the negative. They deal with the not so good things that happen in education.

In this course we will focus on trends and issues in education.

       If I ask you what one factor causes the change in the education, today? I hope most of you will
come up with technology. In twenty first century even yet we are using yesterdays’ training with today’s
students. To be compatible with twenty first century education we have to give technology due
importance.

        We have to see what trends we have to study in technology and what issues in technology we
would talk about. In order to provide education to each and every child we have to uplift our resources.
We, the teachers of today are basically the product of twentieth century; unlike the students are also
twenty first century students. The teachers have to unlearn the concepts of last century and update
ourselves with twenty first century.

        Education must enable nations and communities to gradually evolve and strengthen their
systems of social justice, democratic institutions, and foster values of peace, harmony, tolerance, and
mutual respect among diverse populations. All these skills are necessary to survive in twenty first
century. Education should also promote individual freedom, empower people and a vehicle to uplift the
economic situation.

Topic 2: International Conventions for Free and Quality Education

Provision of free and quality education has been declared as fundamental rights. They want all children
to get basic elementary, secondary education.

1. Universal declaration of human rights

        This convention was approved by the world nations at the United Nations General Assembly in
        1948. According to this convention everyone has the right to education and education shall be
        free at least in the elementary and fundamental basis.

         Elementary education involves pre-school, the early years and education up to grade 5. It is
supposed to be free. It means that govt. or any other agency shall be sponsoring that. All the children
shall be in school in those grades.

    2. Convention on the rights of the child

          Convention on the rights of the child in 1989 explicitly recognized education as a fundamental
right. All children must be in school progressively meaning gradually. They also have equal opportunity
for all the students. The elements of this convention states make primary education compulsory and
available free to all children. Encourage the development of different forms in secondary education
including general and vocational. Education of a child does not stop at elementary level. Vocational
education helps a student to earn a living.

    3. DAKAR world education forum

        April 2000 164 countries combined together, to ensure Education for All (EFA). They focused at
achieving the goal in developed, developing and under developed countries to achieve till 2015. Pakistan
has not met most of the targets set under that convention.

        EFA Goals

Following are some of the EFA goals with explanation.

       Expanding and improving comprehensive early childhood education. There is a need to
        improve the comprehensive basic education
       Ensuring that by 2015 all students particularly girls and those belonging to the ethnic
        minorities receive an education. 2015 was the target, 15 years were given to countries to plan
        that. We have not met this target. Many of our children are not going to school. We have to see
        what countries have achieved these targets. We have to compare our country with others.
       Ensuring that the learning needs of all young people and adults are met through equitable
        acces to appropriate learning and life skills
                Every child should have equitable access. No child should say that there is no school in
        my area. For that we have to improve our infra-structure
       Achieving 50% improvement in levels of adult literacy by 2015

                    Based on 2000, whatever the adult literacy was then, they wanted that in coming 15
           years it should improve by 50%. Most of our adult population is not literate.
          Eliminating gender disparities in primary and secondary education by 2005
                    Only 5 years were given to remove gender disparity from schools. In 2015 the target was
           set to equalize the gender in schools i.e. to make the same number available for boys and girls.
           We have to look at the countries in our region, the developing countries that have come close to
           achieving the targets.
          Improving all aspects of the quality of education and ensuring excellence of all so that
           recognize and measurable outcomes are achieved by all
                    Improving education, it is not a simple task. By improving education we mean we mean
           to improve the facilities, teacher training, schools, curriculum, examination, and assessment
           system. Unless all that is improved, the quality of education cannot be improved.

       4. Convention Millennium Development Goals (MDGs)

Eight millennium development goals were set by the United Nations for the signatory countries.
Following are the details of those 8 MDGs

   I.      Eradicate extreme poverty and hunger

We need to feed our population through a balanced diet.

  II.      Achieve universal primary education

Lesson No.29
                             RELEVANCE AND PARTICIPATION
Topic 136
Relevance and Participation
Relevance is the raison d’etre of population education. Its goal is to improve learners’ and nations’
abilities to deal effectively with population issues.
This is a most practical concern. The challenge facing population educators is to ensure that, in
translating this goal into action, the program retains its focus on the needs of the learners, their
families, communities and societies.
Furthermore, there is an increasing recognition that learners need to participate more in the various
planning and implementation stages of population education programs but, in most cases their
participation is still more spoken of than practiced. In the absence of mass participation in pre-
program activities, who can stand in for the learners?
How does the educator avoid imposing his perception of need on them? Can efforts to increase
learners’ participation at the local level be generalized when programs are being designed for
provinces/states and regions within countries or when a national program is being planned.
Topic 137
Program Planning/ Implementation
Formal education systems in the developing world and in most industrialized nations are financed
and directed largely from the national center. Deciding how these systems can be responsive to the
needs of learners in different parts of the country, in different racial and ethnic groups, in different
social and economic classes is another problem for population educators.
The academic organization of schools has not always been sufficiently in tune with these
differences, and this has contributed to the recent disillusionment over schooling in many parts of
the world.
Nationally-directed out-of-school programs are also likely to face the same problem unless special
efforts are made to localize their activities. Decentralization, in both school and out-of-school
programs, of teacher training, of program planning, of curriculum and material development is
usually difficult to achieve because of the large-scale programs and the usual shortages of resources.
Topic 138
Future Oriented learning
In school programs, many of the population related decisions likely to be considered are those that
will be made in the future: where to live, when and if to marry, when and if to have children and
so on. Even out-of-school programs for adults educate for future decisions, although this future
may not be distant as it is for many school children.
In addition, the repercussions of these decisions may be spread over a number of years. This
presents special problems for population educators, because the situation may change between
the end of the educational process and the time for decision.
This raises the problem of how best to train for an unknown future, how to reinforce the learning
process so that the content will be better retained, how to emphasize the process of finding
solutions rather than the solutions themselves.
Viewing population education in a lifelong context emphasizes the importance of further
development for both school and out-of-school programs and the need to link these efforts
through all available educational settings and channels. But the linking together of the various parts
of the total educational and learning system of a society --- school and out-of-school ---- is quite a
complex enterprise, still in the first steps of its development.
Topic 139
Persuasion and prescription 1

No education system, anywhere in world is free from some degree of persuasion and prescription,
despite the theoretical commitment to truth telling. Training for citizenship and developing the sense
of being part of a nation usually involves elements of conditioning. Furthermore, no educational
process can be totally value free, because any selection of facts involves conscious and unconscious
value choices.
Population education faces these general problems and is also potentially confronted with a more
direct conflict between theory and practice: the degree to which the educational system can or
should directly support the population policies of the nation.If the government has determined that
the small family shall be the norm, or that migration must take place in order to relieve dense
population, or that country's population should increase, what is the proper and possible role of the
educational system?
Topic 140
Persuasion and prescription 2
Should the system adopt these prescriptions as educational goals? Or should it assume a value- fair
stance in which various points of view are examined (even though some may have more weight
than others) and the decision left to the learners?
Obviously, such a statement of issues is overly simplistic but it helps to focus on one of the key
issues facing the population educator in planning and implementing his program.
And even if it is decided that a prescriptive approach is necessary (either because of the severity of a
population situation because government policy would not permit otherwise), the efficacy of
prescription is, in certain circumstances, questionable.

                                      POPULATION STUDIES
Topic 141
Population Studies
Population education is not an attempt to develop a new discipline. Although demography and folk
demography form the core of knowledge needed for population education, they do not cover the
whole range of issues involved.
Facts, theories and concepts from a broad spectrum of academic disciplines and professional fields
are needed to help individuals and societies fully understand population interactions and thus the
effect of population factors on the quality of their individual and collective lives. The sum of this
knowledge is referred to as population studies.

a) How peaceful are schools and classrooms in Pakistan? In your experience, have schools
   become more or less peaceful in recent years? What makes you say this? (10 marks)

    Education has been touted as one of the most powerful tools we can
    implement in our global efforts to promote world peace.
    Here’s a look at the top ways schools and classrooms peace.
    Education Boosts Confidence & Hope
    Confidence breeds hope. Hope breeds peace.” Confidence has been defined as the belief that
    you can succeed at something and a sense of self assuredness. Knowledge is a key
    confidence builder; it allows one to feel a sense of accomplishment, to be more fearless, and
    to grow in unexpected ways. This confidence and self assuredness in turn sparks motivation
    and optimism—or hope as Confucius says— to work towards peace.

    2 Education Promotes Independent Thinking

Education encourages independent thinking, and it opens doors to new ideas. Independent
thinkers tend to try to make sense of the world and draw their own conclusions instead of
blindly following the beliefs of others. Independent thinkers may be less likely to join
militant groups or be followers, and may instead be leaders towards positive change and
action.

3 Education Inspires Problem Solving Skills
Along with math skills that are learned in classrooms, students are often challenged to use
logical thinking in order to analyze different pieces of literature, the significance of
historical events, and scientific findings. Coupled with independent thinking, these critical
thinking skills can lead to innovative solutions and alternatives to violence.

4 Education Builds Communication Skills
In the classroom, students are often asked to speak or read in front of others, offer opinions,
and break into small groups to work on projects together. This is how communication skills
are honed, and communication is they key to solving conflict. Through quality education,
students may be armed with the tools to work within their communities to solve problems, or
to do so on a global scale.

5 Education Opens Doors
There’s no doubt that education for peace leads to career enhancement, employment
opportunities, and chances of higher earnings. What was once out of reach for girls in the
remote villages we work with—say becoming a doctor or a lawyer—are now possibilities.
And with these careers in place, many come back to work within their communities and
support their families, often promoting peace.

6 Education Reduces Poverty
Imagine always being uncomfortable, malnourished, and fearful, not knowing where your
next meal will come from if it comes at all. This fear can often lead to anger, and anger to
violence. Education, especially when it’s combined with technical training (read more about
CAI’s vocational training programs), has been proven to reduce poverty. This is one driving
force behind education for peace. With education comes knowledge, power, safety, security,
and peace. One study by UNESCO found that income around the world would be 23 percent
higher per capita in countries with education for all. If poverty were reduced, violence would
follow suit.

    7 Education Increases Political Involvement
    Educated citizens are less likely to stand for government corruption and can spur more
    government accountability. For women, education can even the playing field, and they are
    more likely to participate in political discussions, town meetings, and decision making,
    therefore leading to a government that represents its citizens more equally. Because
    educated women are less likely to support terrorism (see number 8), they can promote
    alternatives through politics.

Contemporary Issues and Trends in Education  (EDU401)
Q 1: Critique  the equity issues in the field of education. Suggest the solution to deal with such issues.
Critique of Equity Issues in Education
Equity issues persist on various fronts,
One most important problem is the socioeconomic
Disparity among students.
Education is widely regarded as the cornerstone of societal progress and individual empowerment. However, the field of education is plagued by equity issues that hinder its potential to serve as a truly transformative force. These issues manifest in various forms, including:
    1. Unequal Access to Quality Education:
Many students face disparities in access to resources such as textbooks, technology, and quality teachers . They face limited access to quality education due to factors such as school funding disparities, teacher shortages, and inadequate infrastructure. This inequity perpetuates cycles of poverty and limits social mobility.
    2. Discrimination and Implicit Bias: Discrimination based on race, ethnicity, gender, socioeconomic status, and other factors pervades educational settings. Implicit biases, often unconscious, can lead to unfair treatment and hinder academic achievement for marginalized groups.

    3. Inadequate Funding: Schools in low-income communities often lack funding, Which may result in overcrowded classrooms, outdated resources, and a shortage of qualified teachers.
    4. Lack of Opportunities:Access to high-quality early childhood programs is often limited for children from low-income families, putting them at a disadvantage from the start.
    5. Achievement Gap: There is often a significant disparity in academic achievement among different groups of students, such as based on race, socioeconomic status, or gender.
    6. Cultural Bias in Curriculum: The curriculum in schools may not always reflect the diverse experiences and perspectives of all students. This can result in a lack of cultural representation .
    7. Discipline Disproportionality: There is a persistent issue of disproportionate disciplinary actions towards certain student groups, particularly students of color and those with disabilities. This can lead to negative outcomes such as higher dropout rates and involvement with the criminal justice system.
These are just a few examples of the equity issues present in education. It is important to address these challenges to ensure that all students have equal opportunities to succeed.
Solutions to Address Equity Issues in Education
    1. Increase Funding for Schools : Allocating more resources to schools in underserved areas can help improve facilities, attract qualified teachers, and provide students with the support they need to succeed.
    2. Implement Policies to Promote Diversity and Inclusion: Educational institutions should actively promote diversity and inclusion in their staff, curriculum, and policies. This includes fostering inclusive classroom environments, addressing unconscious biases, and celebrating cultural differences.
    3. Recruit and Retain Qualified Teachers from Diverse Backgrounds: A diverse teaching workforce can better represent the student body and provide culturally sensitive instruction. Policies should encourage recruitment and retention of teachers from marginalized backgrounds.
    4. Develop Alternative Assessments that are More Equitable: Standardized tests should be complemented by alternative assessments that better reflect students' diverse learning styles and strengths. These assessments should be culturally sensitive and avoid perpetuating existing biases.
    5. Provide Early Childhood Education Opportunities for All Children: Universal access to high-quality early childhood education can help level the playing field and prepare all children for success in school and beyond.
Question No:2
Describe the role of conflict resolution in the smooth functioning of an educational institute.
Role of Conflict Resolution in Educational Institutions :
Conflict resolution is super important in schools. It helps solve problems and make the learning environment better.
Its all about communicating well, understanding each other, and finding solutions that everyone agrees on.
Conflict resolution teaches us how to get along, respect each other, and make school a positive place to learn and grow.
plays a crucial role in the smooth functioning of educational institutions.
Effective conflict resolution strategies can help to:
    1. Maintain a Positive and Safe Learning Environment: By addressing conflicts promptly and constructively, schools can promote a sense of safety and respect among students, staff, and parents.
    2. Prevent Bullying and Harassment: Conflict resolution techniques can be used to address bullying and harassment incidents, creating a more inclusive and supportive school environment.
    3. Improve Communication and Collaboration: Effective conflict resolution fosters open communication and collaboration among all stakeholders, leading to better decisionmaking and problem-solving.
    4. Promote Emotional Intelligence and Social Skills: Conflict resolution processes can help students develop emotional intelligence and social skills, enabling them to manage their emotions, communicate effectively, and resolve conflicts peacefully.
    5. Enhance the Overall School Climate: By addressing conflicts effectively, schools can create a more positive and harmonious school climate, conducive to learning and personal growth.

Conflict resolution is really important in schools because it helps solve problems and make things better. When students or teachers have conflicts, they can use conflict resolution to work things out and find solutions that everyone agrees on. Conflict resolution helps create a positive and peaceful environment where everyone can learn and grow together. By teaching students effective conflict resolution skills and implementing proactive conflict resolution strategies, schools can create a positive, inclusive, and productive learning environment for all students.

Topic 113

EU’s Definitions (EC 2001) I

Formal Learning:

Learning typically provided by an education or training institution, structured (in terms of objectives,
learning time or learning support) and leading to certification. Formal learning is intentional from
the learners’ perspective.

Non-Formal Learning:
Learning that is not provided by an education or training institution and typically does not lead to
certification. It is, however, structured (in terms of learning objectives, learning time or learning
support).

Topic 114
EU’s Definitions (EC 2001) II

Non-Formal Learning:

Non-formal learning is intentional from the learner’s perspective.

Informal Learning: learning resulting from daily life activities related to work, family or leisure. It
is not structured (in terms of learning objectives, learning time or learning support) and typically
does not lead to certification.
Informal learning may be intentional but in most cases it is non-intentional (or incidental /
random). EU’s definitions are related with the context of Life-Long Learning policy.

Q1. Billet view of informal learning?
      Billet (2001): There is no such thing as informal learning. All learning takes
      place within social organizations or communities that have formalized
      structures. Informal Learning is organic or holistic, engaging the whole
      person, so that intellect, emotions, values and practical activities are
      blended.
Q2. Privatization Policies in Education ?
The main policies and programs include:
   1. Educational Vouchers
   2. Public School Liberalization
   3. Private Contracting
   4. Tuition Credits and Deductions
   5. Subsidies and Assistance Grants
   6. Home – Schooling
   7. Private Payments
   8. Competition among Schools and Education Agencies
Q3. Demand – Side Pressures ?
   ➢ The first factor that can be cited to explain privatization in education is
      simple: many parents want it. In many countries, education is viewed as an
      important way to gain social and economic advancement.
   ➢ Therefore, the demand for education is high, and if governments cannot
      afford to provide and fund quality education, then parents seek private
      suppliers. This type of demand is ‘excess demand’, over and above what is
      provided by the government. In addition, many parents want for their
      children an education different from that offered in public schools. This is

      ‘differentiated demand’ and it may encourage privatization across all three
      sectors.
   ➢ Both excess and differentiated demand have increased in recent
      decades.Excess demand has grown because education has become more
      important for social and economic betterment: to get high-paying jobs, for
      example, workers must have a high level of skills and credentials that are
      only available from universities.
Differentiated demand has grown for two reasons.
   ➢ One is that many public schools offer education that is standardized or
      uniform. The greater the uniformity in the public schools, the larger the
      number of parents who will seek differentiated demand.
   ➢ The other reason is that economies and societies have become much more
      specialized. Many more trades and occupations have developed, and the
      education system must cater to these.
Q4. General pressure?
There are general pressures to privatize education systems.
   ➢ One such factor is global economic and social change. Globalization, linked
      with market liberalization, has both pressured and encouraged governments
      to seek more efficient, more flexible, and more expansive education systems.
      Privatization may be one response to these changes.
   ➢ Another factor that explains some of the growth in privatization is the
      encouragement of world aid agencies, such as the World Bank. Within the
      last decade, for example, the World Bank has given assistance to countries
      like El Salvador, Indonesia, Mali, the Dominican Republic etc.
Q5. Level and grades of madrassa?
The Madrassa Education system is organized in terms of the following levels and
grades:

  ➢ “ibtidaya” - first to the fifth grades of primary education
  ➢ “mutawasitah” - sixth to eighth grades of middle school
  ➢ “thanviyah-e-ammah” - ninth and tenth grades
  ➢ “thanviyah-e-kassah” - 11th and 12th grades
  ➢ “aliya” - the university Bachelor’s degree (consisting of the 13th and 14th
     years)
  ➢ “alimiyah” - the Master’s degree (being the 15th and 16th years)
  ➢ “takmeel” - advanced post-graduate education
Q6: What is Madrassa Education?
     The term ‘Madrassa’ originates from the Arabic word ‘Darasa’ which means
     ‘To Study’. Madrassa, in general, is referred to the school that imparts
     Knowledge. But in the context of Pakistan or even in Contemporary South
     Asia the term ‘Madrassa’ is often used for Islamic educational institutions
     along with ‘Dar-ul-aloom’ and ‘Jamia’. The main subjects of Madrassa
Education include:
  1. Qur’an
  2. Hadith
  3. Fiqh
Q6. Contemporary concern of population education?
     It is directed at people ---- as individuals or as members of groups, as
     decision-makers or potential decision-makers within their families, as
     citizens within a community, as leaders within a society and as policy
     makers within a nation. All people are population actors, making population
     related decisions throughout their lives. The sum of their decisions shapes
     the nature of population forces (fertility, mortality, migration) which operate
     within a society and which then affect other social, political and economic
     forces. In turn, the population, social, political and economic decisions made

      by the larger mass of people (the society or nation) influence the behavior of
      the individual, the families and the small communities in which they belong.
      Population education in essence, is an educational response to contemporary
      economic, social and political issues.
Q7. Liberalization?
      ‘Privatization’ is also thought of as a ‘liberalization’ --- where agents are
      freed from government regulations, or as ‘marketization’ --- where new
      markets are created as alternatives to government services or state allocation
      systems.
Q8. Two assumptions of Peace education?
   1. Conflict is ubiquitous
   2. There are ways to transform it.

      Peace education is the pedagogical efforts to create a world at peace.

      Peace in its most positive aspects embraces ideas of justice, global
      sustainability and the eradication of structures that promote insecurity:
      poverty, hunger, malnutrition, and lack of access to resources.

Q3. Demand – Side Pressures ?
   ➢ The first factor that can be cited to explain privatization in education is
      simple: many parents want it. In many countries, education is viewed as an
      important way to gain social and economic advancement.
   ➢ Therefore, the demand for education is high, and if governments cannot
      afford to provide and fund quality education, then parents seek private
      suppliers. This type of demand is ‘excess demand’, over and above what is
      provided by the government. In addition, many parents want for their
      children an education different from that offered in public schools. This is

      ‘differentiated demand’ and it may encourage privatization across all three
      sectors.

      decades.Excess demand has grown because education has become more
      important for social and economic betterment: to get high-paying jobs, for
      example, workers must have a high level of skills and credentials that are
      only available from universities.
Differentiated demand has grown for two reasons.
   ➢ One is that many public schools offer education that is standardized or
      uniform. The greater the uniformity in the public schools, the larger the
      number of parents who will seek differentiated demand.
   ➢ The other reason is that economies and societies have become much more
      specialized. Many more trades and occupations have developed, and the
      education system must cater to these.

1. Explain migratory population trend:
Migratory population trends refer to the movement of people from one area to another, typically
for reasons such as employment, education, conflict, or natural disasters. These trends influence
population distribution, urbanization, resource allocation, and social structures in both origin and
destination areas.

2. What is population education?
Population education is an educational program that provides students with knowledge, attitudes,
and skills to understand population issues such as growth, distribution, density, migration, and
their impact on socio-economic development and the environment .

3. What is the link of population studies with other studies?
Population studies intersect with sociology, economics, environmental science, geography, and
public health. For example, understanding population trends is essential for economic planning,
healthcare delivery, and resource management.

4. Relationship between population and media:
Media plays a vital role in creating awareness about population issues such as family planning,
urbanization, and migration. It can shape public opinion and influence policy-making.

5. Contemporary concerns related to population education:
Concerns include overpopulation, youth bulges, declining fertility in some regions, urban
crowding, unemployment, environmental degradation, and access to quality education and
healthcare.

6. What is relevance and participation in population education?
Relevance refers to how well population education aligns with real-world problems. Participation
implies engaging learners actively in discussions and activities that make the content meaningful
and action-oriented.

7. Role of ideological theories and culture in population education:
Ideologies and cultural values shape how societies perceive population issues. For example,
religious or cultural views may affect attitudes toward family size, gender roles, or use of
contraception.

8. How does climate change affect educational planning and content?
Climate change affects school infrastructure (e.g., floods, heatwaves), curriculum (need for
environmental education), and attendance (e.g., displacement or health issues), prompting
schools to adopt sustainable practices and resilience-focused content.

9. Briefly discuss historical traces of population studies:
Population studies have evolved through censuses and demographic surveys dating back
centuries. Modern population education gained traction post-WWII as a response to rapid
population growth and its implications.

10. Level of aggregation in relation with population education:
This refers to the scale of analysis—local, regional, national, or global—used to understand
population data and trends, influencing how policies and education are shaped.

11. Population education related to other studies:
It is directly linked with environmental education, development studies, and public health, as
population dynamics impact resource use, poverty, and wellbeing.

12. Describe knowledge-based economy and how we prepare students:
A knowledge-based economy relies on intellectual capabilities rather than physical inputs. To
prepare students, curricula must focus on critical thinking, digital skills, innovation, and lifelong
learning.

It helps learners make informed decisions about health, family size, and environment, promoting
responsible citizenship and sustainable development .

Why is Privatization Happening
There are many factors driving privatization in education. These factors differ in intensity
between countries and across the three sectors of primary, secondary and tertiary education.
It is worth noting that some advocates of privatization are motivated by an ideological
commitment to individual rights over government intervention. These advocates believe that a
family’s right to choose its own education is paramount.
Why is Privatization Happening
Following are the dominant pressures for Privatization:
1. Demand – Side Pressures
The first factor that can be cited to explain privatization in education is simple: many parents
want it. In many countries, education is viewed as an important way to gain social and economic
advancement.
Therefore, the demand for education is high, and if governments cannot afford to provide and
fund quality education, then parents seek private suppliers.
This type of demand is ‘excess demand’, over and above what is provided by the government.
Why is Privatization Happening
2. Supply-side Pressures

The second factor that motivates privatization is the decline in the quality of, and in some cases
the reductions in funds available to, the public sector.
Many parents may feel that the local public school is inefficient in providing education of the
type that is most needed; this dissatisfaction is reported by parents in very basic terms (such as
the inability of the school to guarantee their children’s safety).
In some cases enrolments have expanded much faster than funding, resulting in overcrowding,
large classes, and double or triple shifts for delivery of instruction. Part of the perceived decline
in quality may be a consequence of a fall in per-student funding.
Higher education often has a high cost per unit, governments expect students to bear an
increasing financial burden for their higher education.
Why is Privatization Happening
3. General Pressures

In addition to these push-and-pull pressures discussed previously, there are general pressures to
privatize education systems. One such factor is global economic and social change.
Globalization, linked with market liberalization, has both pressured and encouraged governments
to seek more efficient, more flexible, and more expansive education

                                           sahil
systems. Privatization may be one response to these changes.
Diversity Private Education Pakistan
Diversity of private education in Pakistan is a characteristic feature and has tremendous
implications for policy research but this aspect remains largely under explored in the literature.
As a result, private sector as the provider of education has generally been treated as a
homogenous category, though to a lesser degree than the public education sector.
Ordinarily, differentiation is made between low- and high-fee schools, Urdu- and English-
medium schools with different syllabi and between boys, girls and mixed schools. However, in
reality the private educational institutions can be classified along a much broader range of
categories.
Financing private Education in Pakistan
The size of private sector engaged in delivery of education services and its rapid growth in terms
of number of institutions, teachers and enrolment draw attention to some fundamental questions
pertaining to financing of private education in Pakistan.
Financing Private Education Pakistan
The data available to answer these and similar questions related to financing of private education
is insufficient and whatever is available is too much scattered.
The deficiency of data is evident from the fact that the most comprehensive set of financing
statistics are available only in the Census of Private Educational Institutions 1999-2000.
Since then, considerable changes might have occurred in trends and patterns of investment,
receipts and expenditure of private educational institutions but it is difficult to analyze those
changes because National Education Census 2005 and NEMIS haven’t collected this
information.

EDU401 GDB SOLUTION

FALL 2022

Educational equity:

Educational equity, also known as equity in education, is a measure of achievement, fairness, and opportunity in
education. The study of education equity is often linked with the study of excellence and equity.

Educational equity depends on two main factors. The first is fairness, which implies that factors specific to one’s
personal conditions should not interfere with the potential of academic success. The second factor is inclusion, which
refers to a comprehensive standard that applies to everyone in a certain education system. These two factors are closely
related and depend on each other for an educational system’s success.

Another Defination:

The quality of education that students receive directly correlates to their quality of life years down the road. Early
education in particular has the power to shape a child’s future and the more resources available to them, the better. For
this reason, it’s crucial for educators to address any barriers young students face to succeeding in school.

An American politician once said, “The problem with our education system is not that parents do not have a choice.
The problem is that inequities continue to exist.”

Major equity issues:

   Inequities occur when biased or unfair policies
   financial differences
   programmes, practices, or situations contribute to a lack of equality in educational performance,
   Unfair results.
   Favouritism among students.
   Prefer to someone’s upon others
   Different nationalities.
   Prefer to race.

How these issues effect educational system:

      Poverty and Homelessness
      Food Insecurity
      Non-fluency in English
      Mental Health Concerns
      Future dissatisfaction
      Lack of confidence.
      Family issues .
      Parent’s priority
      Unambitious.

Maha Malik’s Compilation

 Issues
Issues deal with the negative. They deal with the not so good things that happen in education.
 Madrassa
The term ‘Madrassa’ originates from the Arabic word ‘Darasa’ which means ‘To Study’.
Madrassa, in general, is referred to a school that imparts Knowledge.
 Madrassa Education
As an alternate track to Western style of education, religious seminaries – madaaris and religious
education have played a vital role in the history of Islam to fulfill the education needs of Islamic
society. The Madrassa Education has been prevalent since the time of Prophet Muhammad PBUH
in the Muslim world.
 Peace
By peace, we mean more than the absence of violence (negative peace). Peace in its most positive
aspects embraces ideas of justice, global sustainability and the eradication of structures that
promote insecurity: poverty, hunger, malnutrition, and lack of access to resources.
 Peace education
Peace education is the pedagogical efforts to create a world at peace.
 Racism
the belief that one’s own culture or racial heritage is innately superior to that of others, hence, the
lack of respect or appreciation for those who belong to a different race.
 Religious intolerance
Prejudice against those who are followers of religious other than one’s own.
 Sexism
A system of attitudes, actions and structures that subordinates others on the basis of their sex where
the usual victims are women.
 Silent exclusion
Silent exclusion is the children who come to school yet gain nothing.

?communication -- active listening, self-expression, paraphrasing, reframing ?assertiveness
?ability to cooperate ?affirmation ?critical thinking ?ability to think critically about prejudice
?ability to deal with stereotypes ?dealing with emotions ?problem solving ?ability to generate

on behalf of peace ?ability to live with change

 B.ED Secondary (1.5- Year)
 EDU401:Contemporary Issues and Trends in Education

       HANDOUTS TOPIC NO 1 TO 204

 MUHAMMAD IMRAN

 Lesson 1. Introduction to Contemporary Trends and Issues and National and
 International Conventions on Education

Topic 1: Education in twenty first Century

 In the title of the course there are three (3) key terms.

    1. Contemporary
    2. Trends
    3. Issues

 These three terms can be explained like as under.
    1. Contemporary
    Contemporary means related to the present time or starting as of today. What we experience in
 education today.
    2. Trends
    Are positive kinds of things that are happening in other words the patterns that we like to see
 and continue.
    3. Issues

    Issues deal with the negative. They deal with the not so good things that happen in education.

 In this course we will focus on trends and issues in education.

        If I ask you what one factor causes the change in the education, today? I hope most of you
 will come up with technology. In twenty first century even yet we are using yesterdays’ training with
 today’s students. To be compatible with twenty first century education we have to give technology
 due importance.

       We have to see what trends we have to study in technology and what issues in technology
 we would talk about. In order to provide education to each and every child we have to uplift our
 resources. We, the teachers of today are basically the product of twentieth century; unlike the
 students are also twenty first century students. The teachers have to unlearn the concepts of last
 century and update ourselves with twenty first century.

          Education must enable nations and communities to gradually evolve and strengthen their
 systems of social justice, democratic institutions, and foster values of peace, harmony, tolerance,
 and mutual respect among diverse populations. All these skills are necessary to survive in twenty
 first century. Education should also promote individual freedom, empower people and a vehicle to
 uplift the economic situation.
Topic 2: International Conventions for Free and Quality Education

 Provision of free and quality education has been declared as fundamental rights. They want all
 children to get basic elementary, secondary education.

    1. Universal declaration of human rights

        This convention was approved by the world nations at the United Nations General Assembly
        in 1948. According to this convention everyone has the right to education and education
        shall be free at least in the elementary and fundamental basis.

        Elementary education involves pre-school, the early years and education up to grade 5. It is
 supposed to be free. It means that govt. or any other agency shall be sponsoring that. All the
 children shall be in school in those grades.

                                                                            MUHAMMAD IMRAN        1

           2. Convention on the rights of the child

           Convention on the rights of the child in 1989 explicitly recognized education as a
    fundamental right. All children must be in school progressively meaning gradually. They also have
    equal opportunity for all the students. The elements of this convention states make primary
    education compulsory and available free to all children. Encourage the development of different
    forms in secondary education including general and vocational. Education of a child does not stop
    at elementary level. Vocational education helps a student to earn a living.

           3. DAKAR world education forum

            April 2000 164 countries combined together, to ensure Education for All (EFA). They
    focused at achieving the goal in developed, developing and under developed countries to achieve
    till 2015. Pakistan has not met most of the targets set under that convention.

              EFA Goals

    Following are some of the EFA goals with explanation.

•    Expanding and improving comprehensive early childhood education.
           There is a need to improve the comprehensive basic education
•    Ensuring that by 2015 all students particularly girls and those belonging to the ethnic
     minorities receive an education. 2015 was the target, 15 years were given to countries to plan
     that. We have not met this target. Many of our children are not going to school. We have to see
     what countries have achieved these targets. We have to compare our country with others.
•    Ensuring that the learning needs of all young people and adults are met through equitable
     acces to appropriate learning and life skills
                  Every child should have equitable access. No child should say that there is no school
           in my area. For that we have to improve our infra-structure
•    Achieving 50% improvement in levels of adult literacy by 2015
                  Based on 2000, whatever the adult literacy was then, they wanted that in coming 15
           years it should improve by 50%. Most of our adult population is not literate.
•    Eliminating gender disparities in primary and secondary education by 2005
                  Only 5 years were given to remove gender disparity from schools. In 2015 the target
           was set to equalize the gender in schools i.e. to make the same number available for boys
           and girls. We have to look at the countries in our region, the developing countries that have
           come close to achieving the targets.
•    Improving all aspects of the quality of education and ensuring excellence of all so that
     recognize and measurable outcomes are achieved by all
                  Improving education, it is not a simple task. By improving education we mean we
           mean to improve the facilities, teacher training, schools, curriculum, examination, and
           assessment system. Unless all that is improved, the quality of education cannot be
           improved.

EDU401
 World Literacy and Problems in Literacy:

      World Literacy refers to the ability to read and write in different parts of the world.
      Problems in Literacy include challenges like illiteracy (inability to read/write) or lack of
       access to education, making it difficult for people to become literate.

 Issues in Universal Education: Challenges in providing education to everyone in the world,
like poverty, inequality, and lack of resources, which stop people from accessing quality
education.

 Models of Education: Different ways or systems in which education is structured or
delivered. For example, traditional schools, online learning, or project-based learning.

 EU’s Definition and Formal, Informal, and Non-Formal Learning:

      EU's Definition: The European Union's understanding or description of education and
       learning.
      Formal Learning: Education that takes place in a structured environment like schools,
       with clear goals and certification (e.g., university).
      Informal Learning: Learning that happens outside of formal education settings, like
       through experiences, hobbies, or self-learning.
      Non-Formal Learning: Learning that happens outside schools but in structured settings
       like workshops, community centers, or training sessions.

 Population Education: The study of how population growth, family size, and other
demographic factors impact society and education, helping to create awareness about these
issues.

 Population Debate and Issues: Discussions around population growth, its impact on
resources, environment, and education. It involves concerns like overcrowding, unemployment,
and strain on public services.

 Why Population Education: Teaching about population issues is important to help people
understand the effects of overpopulation, family planning, and sustainable living.

 Relevance and Participation: The importance of education that connects to real-life issues
and encourages active involvement from students in their learning.

 Population Studies: Research about the size, structure, and distribution of populations, and
the factors that affect them, like health, migration, or birth rates.

 Research for Program Development: The process of gathering data and information to
create or improve educational programs.

 Privatization of Education: When private companies or individuals take control of
educational institutions, instead of the government.

 Privatization Policies in Education: Rules and decisions made by governments that allow or
encourage private organizations to run schools and educational services.

 Why is Privatization Happening?: Privatization is happening because some believe private
companies can improve quality, offer more choices, or reduce the burden on the government.

 Privatization in Pakistan: The process of allowing private companies or organizations to
manage schools and educational resources in Pakistan.

 Financing, Diversity, and Evaluating Privatization Programs:

      Financing: How privatized education is funded, often by private investors or school fees.
      Diversity: The variety of educational choices available when privatization happens,
       including different teaching styles and subjects.
      Evaluating Privatization Programs: Assessing how well privatized education is
       working, including looking at quality and access.

 Environmental Education (EE): Teaching about the environment, sustainability, and how to
protect nature, so students understand the importance of environmental conservation.

 Implementing Environmental Education and EE in Environment-Friendly Schools:

      Putting environmental education into practice in schools, especially those designed to be
       eco-friendly, using green practices and teaching sustainability.

 Methods for EE: The different ways to teach environmental education, like through hands-on
activities, field trips, or classroom lessons on nature and conservation.

 Children's Voice I-II: Involving children in discussions and decisions about their education,
so they have a say in what and how they learn.

 Teacher Education: Training and professional development for teachers to improve their
skills and knowledge in teaching.

 EE in the School Area I-VII: Incorporating environmental education throughout various
levels of school, from primary to secondary education.

 Technology Education and Engaging Digital Natives: Teaching students, who are very
familiar with technology (digital natives), how to use it effectively for learning and problem-
solving.

 Paths to Successful Education: The different ways or strategies that lead to effective learning
and achieving educational success.

 Technology-enabled Education: Using technology like computers, online resources, and
educational apps to enhance teaching and learning.

 Challenges and Reforms for Tech-supported Education: Problems in using technology for
education (like lack of access or teacher skills) and the changes needed to improve it.

EDU401
Introduction to Contemporary Trends and Issues in Education

Contemporary trends and issues in education refer to the current challenges, changes, and new
directions within educational systems worldwide. These trends influence how education is
delivered, accessed, and evaluated in modern societies. They also address the evolving demands
of a globalized world, where technological advancements, economic shifts, and societal changes
shape educational frameworks.

Some key contemporary trends include:

   1. Technology Integration: The growing use of digital tools, e-learning platforms, and
      artificial intelligence in the classroom.
   2. Inclusive Education: Efforts to make education accessible to all students, including those
      with disabilities or from marginalized groups.
   3. Globalization and Education: The impact of global interconnectedness on education
      systems, including the movement towards international curricula and student exchange
      programs.
   4. Sustainability in Education: The inclusion of environmental education and the promotion
      of sustainable practices in teaching and learning.
   5. Teacher Professional Development: Emphasis on continuous training and support for
      teachers to improve educational quality.

National and International Conventions on Education

Both national and international conventions play a crucial role in shaping educational systems.
These conventions aim to standardize and protect education rights, promote equal access to
education, and encourage collaborative educational practices.

   1. National Conventions: These are often country-specific policies or frameworks that
      dictate how education should be structured, what the curriculum should include, and how
      students' needs are addressed. Examples include the National Education Policy in many
      countries, which outlines priorities and objectives for improving national education
      systems.
   2. International Conventions: International agreements such as the Universal Declaration
      of Human Rights (1948) and UNESCO’s Education for Sustainable Development or
      the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) set global standards
      for education. These conventions push for access to quality education, gender equality in
      education, and the right to education for all, regardless of socio-economic background,
      race, or ethnicity.

Equity Issues in Education

Equity in education means providing fair access to educational opportunities for all students,
regardless of their background or circumstances. Equity issues include disparities based on race,
gender, income, location, disability, and other factors. These inequalities can manifest in various
forms:

   •   Access to quality education: In many parts of the world, disadvantaged groups (such as
       those in rural areas, ethnic minorities, or low-income families) struggle to access quality
       educational resources.
   •   Educational outcomes: Inequities may also appear in the form of differences in academic
       achievement among students from different socio-economic or cultural backgrounds.

Religious Discrimination and Sociocultural Issues in Education

Religious discrimination and sociocultural issues in education refer to biases or prejudices
against certain religious or cultural groups, which can affect their access to quality education. This
can take the form of:

   •   Curriculum biases: Educational materials and curricula may reflect the perspectives or
       values of dominant religious or cultural groups, marginalizing others.
   •   Exclusion from educational opportunities: Certain religious or cultural communities
       may face barriers to education, either because of societal prejudices or institutionalized
       discrimination.

Addressing these issues involves creating inclusive curricula, promoting intercultural dialogue,
and ensuring equal opportunities for all students.

Free and Accessible Education and Its Benefits

Free and accessible education refers to the idea that all individuals should have the right to
receive an education without financial barriers. Education that is both free and accessible has
multiple benefits:

   1. Social Mobility: Education provides opportunities for individuals to improve their socio-
      economic status, particularly for marginalized groups.
   2. Economic Growth: Educated populations contribute to more skilled workforces, leading
      to higher productivity and economic growth.
   3. Social Equity: Free and accessible education helps bridge the gap between different social
      classes and promotes fairness.

Free and Accessible Education: Key Players, Attitudes, Values, Curricula, &
Empowerment

Several key players are involved in promoting free and accessible education:

   •   Governments: They are responsible for funding public education, creating policies that
       promote access, and ensuring that education is free or affordable for all citizens.
   •   Educational Institutions: Schools, colleges, and universities implement the curriculum
       and offer support to all students.
   •   Teachers: Play a central role in delivering quality education and fostering an inclusive
       learning environment.
   •   Students and Families: Students need to be motivated to attend school, and families often
       play a significant role in advocating for their children’s education.

Attitudes and Values: There is an increasing recognition of the importance of education for
personal and societal development, leading to values such as:

   •   Equal Opportunity: Ensuring all students, regardless of background, have the chance to
       succeed.
   •   Empowerment: Education empowers individuals to make informed decisions, participate
       in society, and contribute to economic and social development.

Curriculum: The curriculum should be inclusive and reflect diverse perspectives, promoting the
development of skills, knowledge, and values that contribute to a better society.

Thomas kilman conflict properties, write in your own words.

The Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument (TKI) assesses individuals' preferences in

handling conflicts. It identifies five primary conflict-handling styles: competing,

collaborating, compromising, avoiding, and accommodating. Each style represents a

different approach to conflict resolution based on assertiveness and cooperativeness.

Understanding one's preferred style can help navigate conflicts effectively by adapting

strategies to the situation and the individuals involved. The TKI provides valuable insights

into how individuals respond to conflicts and offers strategies for enhancing

communication and collaboration in various contexts.

Education in Pakistan?

Education in Pakistan faces challenges such as inadequate infrastructure, insufficient

funding, and low literacy rates, particularly in rural areas. The education system is divided

      the best way of cooperation from government side.
   4. Obstacles of bureaucracy for registration of madaaris should be removed
      in the registration process.
   5. Opportunities should be provided for madaaris students for easy
      admission in universities and participation in competitive exams.
   6. The government should provide opportunities of job to wafaq students in
      all its departments.

   Gender disparity in education?

 Gender disparities persist in education. Girls often face barriers like early
 marriage, cultural norms, and lack of resources. Efforts are ongoing to ensure
 equal access to education for both girls and boys.
Role of religion in equity?
Religion can play a significant role in promoting equity in education by
influencing values, beliefs, and practices that support equal access to education

    Edu401 midterm papers

for all individuals. In many cultures, religious teachings emphasize the
importance of justice, compassion, and equality, which can translate into efforts
to ensure that educational opportunities are accessible to everyone regardless of
their background or circumstances. Religious organizations often run schools
and educational programs that cater to marginalized or disadvantaged
communities, providing them with the resources and support needed to access
quality education. These initiatives can help bridge the gap between privileged
and underprivileged students, promoting equity in education.

Mdraasa and politics?
Religious schools, known as madrassas, play a significant role in Pakistani
politics, especially through their connections with religious political parties.
These parties, representing different sects like Deobandis, Barelvis, Ahl-e-
Hadith, and Shia, have strong ties to specific madrassas. A study found that a
majority of madrassas have political affiliations, with most linked to religious
political parties. While some madrassa boards prefer to stay apolitical, others like
Rabita ul-Madaris support specific political parties. It is suggested that students
focus on their education and avoid active political involvement until completing
their studies to maintain a balance between education and politics.
Q. Peace education history elements?
The history of peace education includes efforts after major conflicts, like the
World Wars, to teach people how to resolve disputes without violence. Key
elements involve teaching about human rights, promoting understanding and
tolerance among different cultures, and developing skills for conflict resolution.
 Literacy
  Literacy is the ability to read and write. Efforts to improve literacy rates are
  crucial for education, knowledge, and economic participation.
Impact of Literacy on social environment?
When people can read and write, they can better understand information, communicate
effectively, and participate in society. Higher literacy rates can lead to more informed citizens,
improved economic opportunities, and a stronger sense of community. It helps reduce poverty
and promotes social equality.

Explain education systems of Pakistan in your own words?
The education system in Pakistan includes public and private schools, with
education offered from primary to higher levels. It follows a curriculum set by
the government, but the quality and resources can vary widely between urban and

include access, quality, and funding

edu401-quiz-3-spring-2023-solved-by-vuhe:
EDU401 QUIZ 3 SPRING 2023
                              SOLVED BY SIR ZAHID

                  FOR PAID QUIZ WHATSAPP US 03342743020
1.What is given to the population education at the present stage due to the
difference in goals an objectives?
1.unity
2.entity
3.identity
4.unit
The correct answer is:
3. identity
At the present stage, population education is given a separate identity due to the
differences in goals and objectives from other educational activities like sex
education, family life education, environmental education, and development
education.

2.Population education is bound to reinforce which of the following for
innovation and renovations as the system is already using formal and learner
oriented approaches?
1.
problems
2.issues
3.
trends
4.

solutions
The correct answer is:
3. trends
Population education is bound to reinforce trends for innovation and renovations,
as the system is already using formal and learner-oriented approaches.

3.Privatization is also thought of as a ______________
1.secularism
2.pragmatism
3.Liberalization
4.idealism
The correct answer is:
3. Liberalization
Privatization is also thought of as liberalization, where agents are freed from
government regulations or restrictions.

4.If it is decided that a prescriptive approach is necessary the efficacy of
prescription is, in certain circumstances, _______________.
1.questionable
2.answerable
3.easy
4.difficult
The correct answer is:
Questionable
If it is decided that a prescriptive approach is necessary, the efficacy of
prescription is, in certain circumstances, questionable.

5.There are ___________ forms of Privatization
1.3
2.5
3.4
4.6
The correct answer is:
3
There are three forms of privatization, as mentioned in the provided paragraphs.

6.Methodological issues are concerned which of the following factor for
different ways of adding population education to the school curriculum?
1.Effectiveness
2.Subjectivity
3.Efficiency
4.Objectivity
The correct answer is:
Effectiveness
Methodological issues are concerned with the effectiveness of different ways of
adding population education to the school curriculum.

7.many of the earlier _____________ for school programs emphasized world
and national issues
1.channels
2.sports

3.curricula
4.news
The correct answer is:
3. curricula
Many of the earlier curricula for school programs emphasized world and national
issues.

8.Educational institutions in all countries should be encouraged to expand their
_______________ to include a study of population dynamics and policies.
1.economy
2.education
3.Curricula
4.political system
The correct answer is:
3. Curricula
Educational institutions in all countries should be encouraged to expand their
curricula to include a study of population dynamics and policies.

9.What is the purpose of initiating broader Research Agenda for better and
rational planning of future programs?
1.
problems
2.
program development
3.
mistakes

4.
theory
The correct answer is:
2. program developmenT
The purpose of initiating a broader research agenda is for better and rational
planning of future programs.

10.The continued absence of which factor is appeared as one of the major
barriers for further progress in conceptual and methodological development of
population education?
1.
practice
2.development
3.theory
4.research
The correct answer is:
4. research
The continued absence of research findings in certain areas is considered one of
the major barriers to further progress in the conceptual and methodological
development of population education.

11.In the “World Population Plan of Action”, ____________ rights are
recognized.
1.men’s
2.peoples
3.human

4.women’s
The correct answer is:
4. women's
In the "World Population Plan of Action," women's rights are recognized.

12.What is an important goal that is often suggested for population education?
1.
re-structure
2.reconciliation
3.
recovery
4.renovation
The correct answer is:
4. renovation
An important goal often suggested for population education is to contribute to
educational renovation and innovation by introducing new content and
methodologies.

13.What is the aimed behind most of motivational activities to support?
1.
mortality
2.
funeral
3.
family-planning

4.death-birth rate
The correct answer is:
3. family-planning
Most of the motivational activities aim to support family-planning activities,
encouraging individuals and families to plan and control the size of their families.

14.The population education involves relation to sex education, family life
education, environmental education and which one of the following factor?
1.
growth
2.
development
3.
Enhancement
4.Professional
The correct answer is:
2. development
Population education involves relations to sex education, family life education,
environmental education, and development education.

15.Before passing on to the question of_____________, it seems necessary to
indicate briefly the goals of both population education and other educational
programs
1.contribution
2.integration
3.population

4.disintegration
The correct answer is:
2. integration
Before passing on to the question of integration, it seems necessary to indicate
briefly the goals of both population education and other educational programs.

16.Family, kin, peers and community play a dominant role in acquisition of a
_________ demography
1.community
2.freedom
3.folk
4.personal
The correct answer is:
3. folk
Family, kin, peers, and community play a dominant role in the acquisition of a folk
demography.

17.Programs of _____________ education can contribute to solve either the
population or the educational problems faced by individuals and nations
1.economy
2.human rights
3.population
4.political
The correct answer is:
3. population

Programs of population education can contribute to solving either the population
or the educational problems faced by individuals and nations.

18.Science in inherently masculine in its structure, epistemology and:
1.
Ontology
2. Nature
3.Axiology
4.Methodology
The correct answer is:
3. Axiology

EDU401 RECENT PAPER QUESTIONS
                             COMPILED BY NUMRA KHALID
Q1. Literacy
People also ask how you define literacy. Literacy is the ability to read, write, speak and listen in
a way that lets us communicate effectively and make sense of the world. The current literacy rate
of Pakistan is 62.3 which mean that an estimated population of 60 million is illiterate in the
country.
Q2. Universal declaration of human rights
(The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is an international document adopted by the United
Nations General Assembly that enshrines the rights and freedoms of all human beings.)
Q3. Conflict instruments
 (The Thomas-Kilmann Instrument is designed to measure a person's behavior in conflict
situations. According to the Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument (TKI), used by human
resource (HR) professionals around the world, there are five major styles of conflict
management—collaborating, competing, avoiding, accommodating, and compromising.)
Q4. Note on Madrassa education in Pakistan
 (Madrasa education in Pakistan is one of the prime teaching systems. It gives students religious
education and also teaches them about the lesson of the Quran. They also get to know beliefs and
religious books. This starts soon after they get a basic understanding. Students from all age
groups can enroll in Madrasa. During the 10th century, madrasas emerged as independent
institutions, distinct from mosques, which helped to create a new type of educational system. As
a result, these madrasas became centers for religious and secular learning, as well as places
where officials were educated according to Muslim orthodoxy. )
 Q5. Constitution 1973 about 37B
(In 1973, Article 37-B of the Pakistani Constitution was created, stating that "The State shall
remove illiteracy and provide free and compulsory secondary education within minimum
possible period." Also created in 1973 was Article 38-D of the Pakistani Constitution, which
states "The State shall provide basic education.)
Q6. What is the core madrassa institution?
(The most common of these schools is known as a madrasa. In general, madrasas focus on
teaching the Qur'an, the recorded sayings of the Prophet Muhammad, sacred law and other
Islamic subjects. Most madrassas teach mostly Islamic subjects such as tafseer (interpretation of
the Quran), hadith (thousands of sayings of Muhammad), fiqh (Islamic law) and Arabic (the
language of the Quran); but include some non-Islamic subjects (such as logic, philosophy,
mathematics), which enable students to understand the religious one.)

Q7. Level of literacy
 (The OECD defines literacy across six levels. People with Level 1 or below literacy skills are
considered to have very poor literacy skills, while Level 3 is considered the minimum literacy
skills required for coping with everyday life.)
Q8. Obstacle of free education
 (The problems associated with the education system of Pakistan are lack of adequate budget,
lack of policy implementation, defective examination system, poor physical facilities, lack of
teacher quality, lack of implementation of education policies, directionless education, low
enrollment, high scale dropouts, political)
